cards.objective: Recognise a scaphoid fracture from its mechanism and site of tenderness.
cards.front: A student falls on an outstretched hand and has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. Which bone is most likely fractured?

why.t: The scaphoid links the proximal and distal rows of carpal bones and meets the radius directly, so it takes much of the force of a fall on the outstretched hand. It lies in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox, so tenderness there points to it.
why.check: “Links the two rows” and “floor of the anatomical snuffbox” are not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

simpler.t: The scaphoid is the wrist bone on the thumb side that meets the radius, so a fall onto the hand loads it heavily. It sits under the small hollow at the base of the thumb, so pain there suggests it is broken.
simpler.check: The hollow at the base of the thumb (snuffbox) is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

depth.t: The most commonly fractured carpal bone.
Its blood supply (from branches of the radial artery) enters mainly at the distal end.
So a fracture across the waist can cut off the supply to the proximal pole.
Risk: avascular necrosis and non-union of the proximal fragment.
depth.check: OpenStax says “bone necrosis”; “non-union” and “proximal fragment” need an approved source.

depth.t: The first X-ray can look normal; a later X-ray, once the swelling settles, shows the fracture.

clinical.t: A missed scaphoid fracture can lead to avascular necrosis and later degenerative arthritis of the wrist, because its blood supply is poor. That is why a suspected fracture is treated with caution even when the first X-ray is clear.

trap.t: Do not confuse it with a Colles’ fracture of the distal radius: also from a fall on the outstretched hand, but with a “dinner fork” deformity above the wrist rather than snuffbox tenderness.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e, 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb

cards.objective: Name the nerve that lies directly posterior to the medial epicondyle.
cards.front: Which nerve lies directly posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus?

why.t: The ulnar nerve runs in a shallow groove on the back of the medial epicondyle, covered only by skin and fascia. That is why a knock there sends tingling down the little-finger side of the hand.

simpler.t: The nerve passes right behind the bony bump on the inner side of the elbow, just under the skin, so hitting it makes the little finger tingle.

depth.t: The medial epicondyle is the origin of the powerful anterior forearm (grasping) muscles.
The nerve enters the forearm between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris.
It supplies most of the small (intrinsic) muscles of the hand.
It gives sensation to the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger.

clinical.t: A fracture of the medial epicondyle, or long pressure on the elbow, can injure the ulnar nerve, weakening the small muscles of the hand and numbing the little finger.

hook.t: The “funny bone” is not a bone: it is the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle.

trap.t: Only the ulnar nerve lies behind the medial epicondyle: the median nerve crosses in front of the elbow, and the radial nerve lies on the lateral side.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e, 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (bone); nerve relations await an approved source

cards.objective: Explain the main mechanical role of the clavicle.
cards.front: What is the main mechanical role of the clavicle?
cards.answer: A strut holding the shoulder out from the trunk

why.t: Anchored by muscles from above, the clavicle reaches out to support the scapula, holding the shoulder joint up and away from the trunk. This gives the upper limb its wide range of movement, and passes forces from the limb to the sternum and axial skeleton.

simpler.t: The collarbone works like a prop: it holds the shoulder out to the side, so the arm can move freely, and passes knocks on the arm to the breastbone.

depth.t: The only long bone that lies horizontally.
Sternoclavicular joint: the only bony joint between the upper limb and the axial skeleton.
Its lateral (acromial) end articulates with the acromion of the scapula.
The costoclavicular ligament to the first rib supports the sternoclavicular joint.
It protects the nerves and vessels passing between the trunk and the upper limb.

clinical.t: The clavicle is the most commonly fractured bone, usually between its middle and lateral parts. With the strut broken, the shoulder drops under the weight of the limb, so the patient supports the arm with the other hand.

trap.t: The upper limb’s only bony link to the axial skeleton is the sternoclavicular joint, not the shoulder (glenohumeral) joint.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e, 8.1 The Pectoral Girdle

cards.objective: State which forearm bone is lateral in the anatomical position.
cards.front: Radius or ulna: which is lateral in the anatomical position?

why.t: In the anatomical position the palm faces forward, so the thumb points laterally. The radius runs on the thumb side of the forearm, parallel to the ulna on the little-finger side.

simpler.t: Stand with your palms facing forward: the radius is the forearm bone on the thumb side, on the outside.

depth.t: The radial head articulates with the capitulum of the humerus.
The ulna’s trochlear notch articulates with the trochlea, the main hinge of the elbow.
Distally the radius forms the wrist joint with the scaphoid and lunate; the ulna does not touch the carpal bones.
The radial styloid reaches further distally than the ulnar styloid.

clinical.t: A Colles’ fracture of the distal radius, the most common forearm fracture, follows a fall on the outstretched hand. The distal fragment is driven backwards and upwards, giving the wrist its “dinner fork” bend.

trap.t: In pronation the radius crosses over the ulna, but sides are always named in the anatomical position, where the radius is lateral.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e, 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb; 9.5 Types of Body Movements

cards.objective: Name the nerve at risk in a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus.
cards.front: Which nerve is most at risk in a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus?

why.t: The surgical neck is where the expanded upper end of the humerus narrows into the shaft, and it is a common site of fracture. The axillary nerve wraps around the back of this neck, so a fracture here can stretch or tear it.
why.check: The course of the axillary nerve is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

simpler.t: The surgical neck is the narrow part just below the ball of the humerus. A nerve wraps around it, so breaking the bone there can damage the nerve.
simpler.check: The course of the axillary nerve is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

depth.t: A fall can drive the shaft into the head: an impacted fracture.
The posterior circumflex humeral artery runs around the neck with the nerve.
depth.check: OpenStax mentions the humeral circumflex arteries near the head of the humerus; that the posterior one winds around the surgical neck with the axillary nerve is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

depth.t: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor.
It supplies the skin over the lower deltoid (the “regimental badge” area).
Lower down, the radial nerve lies in the radial groove, at risk in shaft fractures.

clinical.t: Damage to the axillary nerve weakens the deltoid, so raising the arm out to the side is weak, with numbness over the lower outer shoulder.

trap.t: Surgical neck (below the tubercles, often fractured, axillary nerve) is not the anatomical neck (the margin of the smooth head).

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e, 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (bone); nerve relations await an approved source

cards.objective: State what forms the roof of the carpal tunnel.
cards.front: What forms the roof of the carpal tunnel?

why.t: The carpal bones form a U-shaped grouping that makes the walls and floor of the tunnel. The flexor retinaculum, a strong ligament, spans the top of the U as the roof and holds the bones in their arch.

simpler.t: The wrist bones make a U shape. A strong band across the top of the U closes it into a tunnel.

depth.t: Attached laterally to the scaphoid and trapezium, and medially to the hamate and pisiform.
Carries nine tendons from three muscles, plus the median nerve.
depth.check: OpenStax 8.2 says “tendons of nine muscles” and does not name the nerve. The reviewer gives nine tendons from three muscles, plus the median nerve; this needs an approved source.

depth.t: Flexor digitorum superficialis (four), flexor digitorum profundus (four) and flexor pollicis longus (one).
depth.check: OpenStax 8.2 says “tendons of nine muscles” and does not name the nerve. The reviewer gives nine tendons from three muscles, plus the median nerve; this needs an approved source.

depth.t: Overuse or injury can make the contents swell inside this fixed space.

clinical.t: Swelling in the tunnel compresses the median nerve: carpal tunnel syndrome, with pain or numbness and weakness in the parts of the hand it supplies. The bony walls and tough roof cannot stretch, so any swelling squeezes the nerve.
clinical.check: OpenStax does not name the nerve; “median” needs an approved source.

trap.t: The flexor retinaculum is the roof, not the floor: the carpal bones form the floor and walls.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e, 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb. On review, Atlas lists the tunnel’s contents as nine tendons from three muscles, plus the median nerve (OpenStax: “tendons of nine muscles”).

cards.objective: Identify the capitate on the skeleton.

why.t: The head-shaped bone in the centre of the wrist, third in the second row of carpal bones (capitate). It mainly meets the third metacarpal, the palm bone of the middle finger.

simpler.t: The capitate is the wrist bone in the middle of your wrist.

depth.t: Rounded head: its upper end is rounded, fitting a hollow formed by the scaphoid and lunate.
depth.check: OpenStax gives its name and its joints with the scaphoid and lunate; the rounded head fitting their hollow is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

depth.t: Surface for the third metacarpal: its lower surface, at the carpometacarpal joint.
Side surfaces: it meets the trapezoid on the thumb side and the hamate on the other.

clinical.t: A violent fall onto the hand with the wrist bent far back. The capitate and the rest of the hand dislocate backwards around the lunate (perilunate dislocation). The lunate stays attached to the radius while the ligaments around it tear.

trap.t: The capitate is third in the distal row from the thumb side, between the trapezoid and the hamate.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (and glossary); 8.5; 9.4

cards.objective: Identify the clavicle on the skeleton.

why.t: The S-shaped collarbone at the front of the shoulder, joining the arm to the trunk (clavicle). It is the only long bone in the body that lies horizontally.

simpler.t: The clavicle is your collarbone.

depth.t: Shaft: the curved middle part between the two ends.
Underside of the acromial end: the strong coracoclavicular ligament anchors here, tying it to the coracoid process.
Near the sternal end: the costoclavicular ligament ties it to the first rib below.

clinical.t: A fall onto the outstretched arms, or a strong blow to the side of the shoulder. The clavicle breaks, usually between its middle and outer parts. It is the bone broken most often.

trap.t: The clavicle forms from membrane, not cartilage: the only limb or girdle bone to do so.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.1 The Pectoral Girdle; 8.5; 9.4; 20.5

cards.objective: Identify the hamate on the skeleton.

why.t: The hooked wrist bone on the little-finger side, fourth in the second row of carpal bones (hamate). A hook projects from its front, and it anchors the inner end of the flexor retinaculum.

simpler.t: The hamate is the wrist bone below your ring and little fingers.

depth.t: Hook of the hamate: a prominent bony extension on its front.
Surfaces for the fourth and fifth metacarpals: its lower surface, at the carpometacarpal joints.
Upper surfaces: it meets the lunate and triquetrum above.
Side surface: it meets the capitate on the thumb side.

clinical.t: A golf club, bat or racquet handle strikes the base of the palm. The hook of the hamate breaks. The handle presses directly on the hook, which projects forwards.

trap.t: The hamate carries the fourth and fifth metacarpals; the capitate carries mainly the third.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (and glossary); 8.5; 9.4

cards.objective: State the phalanges of the thumb.
cards.front: How many phalanges does the thumb have?

why.t: The thumb (digit 1) has two: a proximal and a distal phalanx. Each finger, digits 2 to 5, has three: proximal, middle and distal.

simpler.t: The phalanges are the bones of your fingers and thumb.

depth.t: Proximal phalanges: the nearest to the palm; each meets a metacarpal head at a knuckle joint.
Middle phalanges: only in the fingers, between the proximal and distal phalanges.
Distal phalanges: the tips of the fingers and thumb.
Interphalangeal joints: the joints between neighbouring phalanges.
Base, shaft and head: each phalanx has a base nearest the palm, a shaft and a head.

clinical.t: A child’s injured finger has an X-ray. There may be no injury: each phalanx has a normal growth plate. Cartilage is less dense than bone, so a normal plate looks dark and can be mistaken for a break.

trap.t: The thumb has two phalanges, with no middle phalanx; each finger has three.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (and glossary); 8.5; 9.4; 9.5; 20.5

cards.objective: Identify the humerus on the skeleton.

why.t: The long bone of the upper arm, running from the shoulder to the elbow (humerus). It is a long bone: a hollow shaft (diaphysis) with a wider end at each end (epiphysis).

simpler.t: The humerus is the bone of your upper arm.

depth.t: Its round head faces inwards (medially) and fits the shallow socket of the shoulder blade.
At the elbow it meets the ulna on the inner side and the radius on the outer side.
Head: the large, smooth, round top.

clinical.t: A fall onto the hand or elbow breaks the bone across the surgical neck. The narrow neck is where the wide top meets the shaft, so force concentrates there.

trap.t: The surgical neck, not the anatomical neck, is the common fracture site.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb; 8.5; 9.6; 20.5

cards.objective: Identify the lunate on the skeleton.

why.t: A moon-shaped wrist bone in the middle of the first row of carpal bones (lunate). With the scaphoid, it is one of only two carpal bones that meet the radius directly.

simpler.t: The lunate is a small wrist bone in the middle of your wrist.

depth.t: Surface for the radius: its upper surface meets the radius directly at the wrist joint.
Surfaces for the second row: its lower surface meets the capitate and hamate at the midcarpal joint.
Side surfaces: it meets the scaphoid on the thumb side and the triquetrum on the other.

clinical.t: A fall onto the outstretched hand with the wrist bent far back. The lunate dislocates forwards, into the carpal tunnel. The dislocated bone takes up space in the tunnel and presses on the median nerve.

trap.t: The lunate meets the radius directly; the triquetrum beside it meets the articular disc instead.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (and glossary); 8.5; 9.4

cards.objective: State which metacarpals are immobile.
cards.front: Which metacarpals are firmly anchored and do not move?

why.t: The second and third are fixed, giving the palm a firm middle. The fourth and fifth move forwards in a power grip, pressing the inner hand against the object.

simpler.t: The metacarpals are the five bones of your palm.

depth.t: Base: the upper end, which meets a carpal bone at a carpometacarpal joint.
Shaft: the long middle part of each bone.
Head: the expanded lower end, which forms a knuckle.
Second and third metacarpals: firmly anchored, so they do not move.
Fourth and fifth metacarpals: can move a little forwards and backwards; the fifth moves most.

clinical.t: A punch that lands on a hard object. The neck of the fifth metacarpal breaks (“boxer’s fracture”). The fifth metacarpal is the most mobile of the palm bones and takes the force of a badly aimed punch.
clinical.check: The fracture is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20); the mobility of the fifth metacarpal is.

trap.t: The metacarpals are numbered from the thumb: the first is at the base of the thumb.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (and glossary); 8.5; 9.4; 9.5; 20.5

cards.objective: Identify the pisiform on the skeleton.

why.t: A small pea-shaped bone on the front of the triquetrum, at the base of the hand (pisiform). It sits on the front of the triquetrum, not in line with the other bones of its row.

simpler.t: The pisiform is the small round wrist bone at the base of your palm, on the little-finger side.

depth.t: Facet for the triquetrum: a flat surface on its back, where it meets the triquetrum.
Front surface: projects forwards, so you can feel it at the base of the hand.
Attachment of the flexor retinaculum: the inner end of the flexor retinaculum anchors to it.

clinical.t: A fall onto the heel of the hand on the little-finger side. The pisiform breaks. A forearm muscle tendon attaches to it and pulls on the broken bone.

trap.t: The pisiform sits on the triquetrum, not on the hamate, though both are on the little-finger side.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (and glossary); 8.5

cards.objective: Identify the radius on the skeleton.

why.t: The lateral bone of the forearm, on the thumb side (radius). It turns around the ulna as the palm turns backwards and forwards (pronation and supination).

simpler.t: The radius is the forearm bone on the thumb side.

depth.t: Neck: the narrow part just below the head.
Radial tuberosity: an oval bump below the neck, on the inner side, where a muscle attaches.
Ulnar notch: a shallow hollow at the lower end that meets the head of the ulna.

clinical.t: A fall onto the outstretched hand, often in an older person with osteoporosis. The lower end of the radius breaks across, and the lower fragment is pushed backwards and upwards (Colles fracture). The hand is carried backwards with the displaced fragment.

trap.t: The radius is lateral (thumb side), and its head is at the elbow, not the wrist.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb; 8.5; 9.4; 9.5; 9.6; 20.5

cards.objective: Identify the scaphoid on the skeleton.

why.t: A small boat-shaped wrist bone on the thumb side of the first row of carpal bones (scaphoid). The scaphoid and lunate meet the radius at the wrist joint; the triquetrum meets the articular disc over the ulna.

simpler.t: The scaphoid is a small wrist bone at the base of the thumb.

depth.t: Surface for the radius: it meets the end of the radius directly at the wrist joint.
Front (palmar) surface: it anchors the flexor retinaculum, the band that roofs the carpal tunnel.
Below it are the trapezium, trapezoid and capitate of the second row.

clinical.t: A scaphoid fracture is missed because the first X-ray looks normal. It affects the bone itself, which has a poor blood supply. With little blood reaching it, the broken bone heals slowly.

trap.t: Only the scaphoid and lunate meet the radius directly; the triquetrum meets the articular disc.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb; 8.5

cards.objective: Identify the scapula on the skeleton.

why.t: The flat, triangular shoulder blade at the back of the shoulder (scapula). With the clavicle it forms the shoulder (pectoral) girdle, which anchors the arm to the trunk.

simpler.t: The scapula is your shoulder blade.

depth.t: Glenoid cavity: the shallow socket for the head of the humerus.
Supraglenoid and infraglenoid tubercles: small bumps above and below the socket, for arm muscles.
Muscles lie in front of it and behind it, so it does not touch the ribs.

clinical.t: A strong blow to the outer shoulder, such as a player driven into the boards. The acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments tear (a “shoulder separation”). The scapula separates from the clavicle and the weight of the arm pulls it down.

trap.t: The acromion forms the tip of the shoulder; the coracoid process is the hook at the front.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.1 The Pectoral Girdle; 8.5; 9.6

cards.objective: Identify the trapezium on the skeleton.

why.t: The wrist bone at the base of the thumb, first in the second row of carpal bones (trapezium). Its saddle joint with the first metacarpal gives humans their opposable thumbs.

simpler.t: The trapezium is the wrist bone at the base of your thumb.

depth.t: Saddle surface: its surface for the first metacarpal is saddle-shaped: concave one way and convex the other.
Surface for the second metacarpal: a small surface beside it, for the second metacarpal.
Surfaces for the scaphoid and trapezoid: it meets the scaphoid above and the trapezoid beside it.
Front surface: with the scaphoid, it anchors the outer end of the flexor retinaculum.

clinical.t: An injury to the joint at the base of the thumb. It affects the first carpometacarpal (saddle) joint. Opposition is produced at this joint, by flexion and abduction of the thumb.

trap.t: The trapezium is next to the thumb; the trapezoid is beside it, towards the index finger.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (and glossary); 8.5; 9.4; 9.5

cards.objective: Identify the trapezoid on the skeleton.

why.t: A small wrist bone at the base of the index finger, second in the second row of carpal bones (trapezoid). It meets only one metacarpal, the second, which is firmly anchored and does not move.

simpler.t: The trapezoid is a small wrist bone at the base of your index finger.

depth.t: Surface for the second metacarpal: its lower surface, at the carpometacarpal joint.
Surface for the scaphoid: its upper surface.
Side surfaces: it meets the trapezium on one side and the capitate on the other.

clinical.t: A hard bony lump on the back of the hand, at the base of the index and middle fingers. There is extra bone (a carpal boss) where the trapezoid and capitate meet the second and third metacarpals. The lump catches the tendons that run over the back of the wrist.

trap.t: The trapezoid meets only the second metacarpal; the trapezium meets the first and second.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (and glossary); 8.5; 9.4

cards.objective: Identify the triquetrum on the skeleton.

why.t: A three-cornered wrist bone, third in the first row of carpal bones (triquetrum). At the wrist joint it meets the articular disc over the ulna, not bone.

simpler.t: The triquetrum is a small wrist bone on the little-finger side.

depth.t: Facet for the pisiform: a small surface on its front, where the pisiform sits.
Surface for the wrist joint: its upper surface meets the articular disc over the ulna.
Surface for the hamate: its lower surface meets the hamate at the midcarpal joint.

clinical.t: A twisting fall on the hand. The articular disc between the ulna and the triquetrum tears. The disc unites the lower ends of the radius and ulna, and the triquetrum presses on it.
clinical.check: OpenStax describes the disc; a tear of the disc in a fall is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

trap.t: The bump you feel at the base of the palm is the pisiform, which sits on the triquetrum.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (and glossary); 8.5; 9.4

cards.objective: Identify the ulna on the skeleton.

why.t: The medial bone of the forearm, on the little-finger side (ulna). Its hooked upper end grips the humerus and forms the hinge of the elbow.

simpler.t: The ulna is the forearm bone on the little-finger side.

depth.t: Radial notch: a small smooth area beside the notch, where the head of the radius turns.
Ulnar tuberosity: a rough area on the front, just below the coronoid process.
Head and styloid process: the small rounded lower end, with a short projection behind it.

clinical.t: Repeated forceful straightening of the forearm, as in baseball pitching. It affects the ulnar collateral ligament on the inner side of the elbow. This ligament stops the elbow moving sideways and over-straightening; its front part resists over-straightening most.

trap.t: The ulna’s head is at the wrist; the bony point of the elbow is the olecranon.

cards.source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb; 8.5; 9.4; 9.5; 9.6; 20.5
